newsitem.title: ZAIRE: War-hit Zaire province gets pro-autonomy governor.
newsitem.headline: War-hit Zaire province gets pro-autonomy governor.

text.p: The popular governor of Zaire's war-ravaged Shaba province, suspended for alleged secession moves two years ago, has been reinstated and vowed on Saturday to protect the regional capital from looting.
"Security of people and goods is my number one priority and the main danger here is looting by bandits," Kyungu wa Kumwanza told reporters in Lubumbashi, Zaire's second largest city.
"We will make sure goods and people are safeguarded day and night. I will add more army patrols around the city."

Fighting has been reported some 220 km (135 miles) from the city of a million people in Shaba, the southeastern region whose riches of copper, cobalt and other minerals have been squandered under President Mobutu Sese Seko's 32-year rule.

Regional security sources said soldiers had clashed with local people waiting for Laurent Kabila's rebels to arrive. They have taken about a quarter of Zaire in five months and, before agreeing to peace talks recently, said Lubumbashi was next.
Even Kyungu admits that Shaba is waiting eagerly for Kabila's rebels to overthrow the government, but what they fear most is looting sparked by soldiers retreating before them.
His pledge to maintain law and order will go down well in the city, whose promising economic ties with southern Africa are growing after decades of decline.
Starting his first full day as governor after Mobutu reinstated him this week, he said he had given up on secession in favour of broad autonomy for his potentially rich region.
"We want immediate change from a centralised to a federal system like in the United States," he said.

A populist leader whose knack for rousing his people led to the driving out of hundreds of thousands of non-Shabans four years ago, he is navigating a careful course between the old order and the rebels who many expect will take over.
"I have no problem with the rebels because I am in a good position with my people. I have been fighting politically for liberation, so the people can enjoy democracy," he said.
The youth wing of his party has been reported to have been involved in clashes with troops in towns in the rebel path, but Kyungu said they were not involved.

Kyungu said he and Kabila were both seeking change, just in different ways. He urged the rebel leader -- who comes from the same village in north Shaba -- to stop fighting and honour an agreement to meet Mobutu's representatives for peace talks.
Kabila, demanding that Mobutu cede power to a transitional rebel government, says he will not work with any politician who served under Mobutu.
But Kyungu, who leads the pro-autonomy UFERI party and whose popularity could ensure him a crucial political role in a new Zaire, said the people would decide that in elections.
"They know I control the whole region and that I can be accepted round the peace table with Mr Kabila," he said.
